title: Can We Trust Eyewitnesses?
context:
A. Most people imagine that memory works like a video camera, storing events exactly as they happened and replaying them on request. Psychologists have shown that this picture is wrong. Remembering is an act of reconstruction: each time we recall an event, the brain rebuilds it from fragments and fills the gaps with what seems likely. These additions feel exactly like genuine memories, and the person recalling them cannot tell which parts are real, which is why honest witnesses can be sincerely mistaken.

B. A well-known series of experiments in the 1970s showed how easily recollections can be altered. Volunteers watched short films of traffic collisions and were then asked to estimate the speed of the cars. Those who were asked how fast the cars had 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates than those who were asked about cars that had 'hit' each other. A week later, the first group were also more likely to say they had seen broken glass, although none appeared in the film.

C. Emotion affects what the mind records. In a violent crime, a witness's attention often fixes on a weapon, leaving little capacity to notice the attacker's face, a phenomenon known as weapon focus. Very high stress can further impair the formation of detailed memories. Surprisingly, the confidence with which a witness speaks is a poor guide to accuracy: studies repeatedly find that people who are certain are wrong almost as often as those who hesitate, yet juries tend to believe the confident.

D. Police often ask witnesses to pick a suspect from a set of photographs or a row of people. Experiments show that if the real culprit is absent, many witnesses choose the person who looks most similar to him instead of saying that nobody matches. To reduce this error, some forces use a double-blind procedure in which the officer running the line-up does not know which person is the suspect, so that he cannot guide the witness by accident. Showing the faces one at a time rather than together also helps.

E. Memory is fragile over time. Much detail is lost in the first hours, and what remains can be altered when witnesses talk to one another, because each person absorbs elements of the others' accounts without noticing. News coverage can have the same effect. For this reason, investigators try to interview witnesses separately and soon after the event, using open invitations such as 'tell me everything you remember' rather than leading questions that suggest an answer.

F. The legal consequences are serious. In the United States, DNA testing has overturned hundreds of convictions, and analysis of those cases shows that mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in the large majority. In response, many courts now give juries a warning that confident testimony is not necessarily accurate, and judges may allow psychologists to explain the research as expert witnesses. Even so, trial lawyers admit that a witness who points at the defendant and says 'it was him' is still extremely persuasive.
